content: In the United States and Canada, the term oatmeal refers to any form of crushed, rolled, or cut oats used in recipes, such as oatmeal cookies. Oatmeal is a product derived from processing oats, typically consisting of coarsely ground, unsifted oats. Rolled oats and steel-cut oats are also commonly referred to as oatmeal. The porridge made from these oats is also called oatmeal or oatmeal cereal. To produce oatmeal, oat groats are coarsely ground, cut into small pieces to create steel-cut oats, or steamed and rolled to make rolled oats. Quick-cooking rolled oats are prepared by cutting the oats into smaller pieces before steaming and rolling. Oatmeal porridge is nutritionally dense, containing higher levels of B vitamins and calories compared to other types of porridge. Beyond its use as a breakfast cereal, oatmeal is incorporated into various products, including alcoholic beverages, cosmetics, soaps, and external medical treatments. It is also used as a flavoring agent in some canned animal products and as a thickener in certain brands of canned chili con carne. Interest in oatmeal has grown in recent years due to its recognized health benefits. Research has demonstrated that consuming a bowl of oatmeal daily can help lower blood cholesterol levels. This health trend gained momentum in the late 1980s, peaking in 1989, but waned by the early 1990s. However, oatmeal's popularity resurged after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's 1997 decision to allow food products high in oat bran or rolled oats to carry labels claiming they may reduce the risk of heart disease when combined with a low-fat diet. This benefit is attributed to the beta-glucan content in oats. Rolled oats have also been a dietary staple for athletes, particularly weight trainers, due to their high levels of complex carbohydrates and fiber, which promote slow digestion and stable blood glucose levels. Despite these developments, the proportion of Americans consuming oatmeal for breakfast has remained unchanged for 20 years, with one in five Americans eating oatmeal. Common additions to oatmeal porridge to enhance its flavor include salt, white or brown sugar, cinnamon, honey, molasses, maple syrup, butter, milk, cream, and various fruits such as strawberries, blueberries, apples, peaches, mangoes, bananas, raisins, dried cherries, and dried cranberries. Nuts, such as pecans and walnuts, are also frequently added, as is peanut butter. In Scotland, oatmeal is produced by grinding oats into a coarse powder, with various grades available depending on the fineness of the grind, including coarse, pinhead, and fine oatmeal. It is used in baking, the preparation of bannocks or oatcakes, as a stuffing for poultry, as a coating for Caboc cheese, and as the main ingredient in traditional Scottish dishes such as skirlie or its deep-fried counterpart, mealy pudding. Oatmeal is also mixed with sheep's blood, salt, and pepper to make Highland black pudding or combined with fat, water, onions, and seasoning, then boiled in a sheep's intestine to create marag geal (Outer Hebridean white pudding), which is often served sliced with fried eggs at breakfast. Traditional porridge, or porage, is another common preparation, as is brose, a thick mixture of uncooked oatmeal with butter or cream, eaten similarly to porridge but more filling. Modern variations often use rolled oats, crushed oats, or instant oats for quicker preparation. Gruel, a thinner mixture made by straining oatmeal mixed with cold water and then heating it, is prepared for infants and invalids. Oatmeal has a long history in Scottish society, as oats are better suited than wheat to the country's short, wet growing season, making them a staple grain. Historically, Scottish universities observed Meal Monday, a holiday allowing students to return to their farms to collect more oats for food. Samuel Johnson disparagingly referred to oats in his dictionary, to which his biographer, James Boswell, a Scot, reportedly retorted. A traditional Scottish method of cooking oatmeal involves soaking it overnight in salted water and cooking it on low heat in the morning until the mixture thickens. In Vermont, oatmeal-making has a long tradition rooted in farm families. Typically, heavy steel-cut oats are soaked overnight in cold water, salt, and maple syrup. Early the next morning, before beginning farm chores, cooks add ground nutmeg, cinnamon, and sometimes ginger to the pot, which is then cooked for up to 90 minutes and served with cream, milk, or butter. As most contemporary Vermonters no longer have farm chores, the recipe has been simplified to a shorter cooking time of 10 to 30 minutes at higher heat. Vermont leads the United States in per capita consumption of cooked oatmeal cereal.
